M4_S01.summary: Of the 121 cittas, 54 belong to the sense sphere, and these divide into 12 unwholesome, 18 rootless and 24 sense-sphere beautiful cittas.
body: Consciousness (Citta) is enumerated as 121 cittas in all: 54 of the sense sphere, 15 of the form sphere, 12 of the formless sphere and 40 supramundane cittas when counted in the extended way.
The 54 sense-sphere cittas fall into three groups: 12 unwholesome cittas, 18 rootless cittas (15 resultants plus 3 functionals) and 24 sense-sphere beautiful cittas.
The 12 unwholesome cittas comprise 8 rooted in greed (Lobha), 2 rooted in hatred (Dosa) and 2 rooted in delusion (Moha).

The fourfold definition of citta: its characteristic is knowing an object; its function is to lead and precede the mental factors; its manifestation is an unbroken continuity, one citta linking to the next; its proximate cause is mentality, materiality and an object.
Four causes bring a citta into being: kamma performed in the past; the presence of an object as condition; the presence of mental factors; and a physical base to depend upon.

M4_S02.summary: The eight greed-rooted cittas are obtained by crossing three pairs — joy or equanimity, with or without wrong view, unprompted or prompted: 2 × 2 × 2 = 8.
body: A greed-rooted citta is consciousness that craves and clings to its object. Its root is lobha, from the root 'lub': to stick fast to, to bind, to cling, to thirst after, to be enamoured of.

The eight greed-rooted cittas are distinguished by three contrasting pairs: joy (somanassa) or equanimity (upekkhā); associated with wrong view (diṭṭhigatasampayutta) or dissociated from wrong view (diṭṭhigatavippayutta); unprompted (asaṅkhārika) or prompted (sasaṅkhārika).
The first of them is named in full: 'Somanassa-sahagataṃ diṭṭhigatasampayuttaṃ asaṅkhārikaṃ' — greed-rooted consciousness accompanied by joy, associated with wrong view, unprompted.

The eight group together in overlapping ways: 1-2-3-4 are accompanied by joy and 5-6-7-8 by equanimity; 1-2-5-6 are associated with wrong view and 3-4-7-8 dissociated from it; 1-3-5-7 are unprompted and 2-4-6-8 prompted.

The weight of their results differs accordingly: joy yields a stronger result than equanimity, unprompted a stronger result than prompted, and association with wrong view a heavier result than dissociation from it.

M4_S03.summary: Both hatred-rooted cittas are accompanied by displeasure and associated with repulsion; they differ only in being unprompted or prompted.
body: A hatred-rooted citta has hatred as its root: its nature is irritation, discomfort, displeasure and dissatisfaction, which in stronger degrees becomes resentment, fury and cruelty.

The first is 'Domanassa-sahagataṃ paṭighasampayuttaṃ asaṅkhārikaṃ' — accompanied by displeasure, associated with repulsion, unprompted. Here displeasure arises together with the citta and a flash of anger springs up at once, without any prompting.
The second is the same but 'sasaṅkhārikaṃ' — prompted: the same anger, but arising more slowly, needing to be urged on by oneself or another.
Displeasure (domanassa) belongs to the aggregate of feeling: it is the uneasy, oppressive, disagreeable way of experiencing an object, and it accompanies only these two cittas.
Four causes give rise to hatred-rooted consciousness: a temperament habituated to anger; failure to reflect deeply; lack of learning and understanding; and repeatedly meeting undesirable objects.

M4_S04.summary: The two delusion-rooted cittas are accompanied by equanimity: one associated with doubt, one with restlessness, both arising from unwise attention and the taints.
body: The first delusion-rooted citta is 'Upekkhā-sahagataṃ vicikicchāsampayuttaṃ' — accompanied by equanimity and associated with doubt; its state is one of wavering, unable to settle.

Doubt occurs at two levels: ordinary doubt about everyday matters, and doubt of the special kind — doubt about the Buddha, the Dhamma, the Sangha, the three trainings (virtue, concentration, wisdom), the past, the future, the present, and dependent origination.
The second delusion-rooted citta is 'Upekkhā-sahagataṃ uddhaccasampayuttaṃ' — accompanied by equanimity and associated with restlessness: the mind is agitated and unsteady, swaying without a footing.

Two causes give rise to delusion-rooted consciousness: (1) unwise attention (ayoniso manasikāra), attention that is not in accordance with the Dhamma or with the facts and so leaves the mind in a fog; and (2) the taints as its foundation — the taints of sensuality, of existence, of views and of ignorance.

M4_S05.summary: The fourteen unwholesome cetasikas are grouped by what they co-arise with: 4 of the delusion group, 3 of the greed group, 4 of the hatred group, 2 of sloth-torpor and doubt alone.
body: Akusala — the unwholesome — carries five senses: diseased, in that it brings pain and suffering; not lovely, that is, bad and defiled; unskilful, with reason clouded by greed, hatred and delusion; faulty, since it does what is mistaken; and productive of suffering, since unwholesome deeds yield painful results.

The 14 unwholesome mental factors fall into five groups: the delusion group of 4 (delusion, shamelessness, fearlessness of wrongdoing, restlessness — studied in module M2), the greed group of 3 (greed, wrong view, conceit), the hatred group of 4 (hatred, envy, avarice, worry), the sloth group of 2 (sloth and torpor), and doubt, which stands alone.
The delusion group is called the unwholesome universals because all four of its factors are present in every one of the twelve unwholesome cittas.

The greed group (Lobhatuka) gathers the factors that co-arise with greed — the mind clinging to its object — into one group. The hatred group (Dosatuka) gathers the factors that co-arise with hatred — the mind striking at its object — into another.

The four remaining groups, unlike the delusion group, are not present in every unwholesome citta: each arises only in the cittas that suit its own object. The details of each group follow in the next sections.

M4_S06.summary: Greed clings to the object, wrong view clings to mistaken opinions about it, and conceit measures oneself against others — the three factors that co-arise with greed.
body: Greed (Lobha) comes from the root 'lub' — to stick fast, to bind, to cling, to thirst, to be enamoured: 'lubhatīti = lobha', what sticks fast is called greed. It is the attitude of clinging to objects taken as good, beautiful, lovely or attractive as they come through the doors of eye, ear, nose, tongue, body and mind.

The fourfold definition of greed: its characteristic is grasping the object; its function is to make the mind stick to the object like meat to a hot pan; its manifestation is not letting the object go; its proximate cause is seeing enjoyment in things that in fact fetter.

A number of words share its meaning: pema (affection), taṇhā (craving), rāga (lust, infatuation), piya (what is dear), kāya (fondness), nandi (delight). Clinging (upādāna) is greed intensified — grasping and holding on with force.

Greed joined with wrong view grasps and holds mistaken opinions: clinging to one's own views and speculations, to superstition and confusion. Greed dissociated from wrong view goes together with conceit: clinging to what is felt to be one's own, with comparison of oneself as better or worse than others.

Wrong view (Diṭṭhi) derives from 'dis' — to see, to know; diṭṭhi is thus a view or opinion. Wrong view (micchā diṭṭhi) is seeing that does not accord with the truth, understanding things through an opinion that contradicts their actual nature.

Personality view (Sakkāyadiṭṭhi) is reckoned by way of the five aggregates, with four modes for each: taking the aggregate of materiality to be the self; seeing materiality inside the self; seeing the self as possessing materiality; seeing the self inside materiality. Four modes × five aggregates (materiality, feeling, perception, formations, consciousness) gives twenty kinds of personality view.

Wrong view is further classified as ordinary wrong view — mistaking things, mistaking what is 'I' and 'mine', mistaking the real nature of phenomena, mistaking spurious teachings for true ones — and wrong view of a definite character: the three fixed wrong views, and the two chief ones, the view of non-causality (holding that nothing has a cause, that everything happens by chance, and so disbelieving kamma and its result) and the nihilistic view (that death is the end and deeds bear no fruit).

Conceit (Māna) comes from the root 'man' — to pile up, to heap one thing upon another. Māna is self-importance, pride, self-exaltation, self-satisfaction, the measuring of oneself against another, arrogance, and equally the inferiority complex. Priding oneself on having more than another is conceit.

Nine kinds of conceit arise from the three comparisons — superior, equal, inferior: the superior person who thinks himself superior, equal or inferior; the equal person who thinks himself superior, equal or inferior; and the inferior person who thinks himself superior, equal or inferior.

Pride can fasten on almost anything: birth, family, health, youth, long life, gain, honour, respect, praise, a following, wealth, beauty, learning, eloquence, virtue, meditative attainment, fame, position, and the rest.

M4_S07.summary: Hatred burns and destroys its object; envy cannot bear another's success, avarice hides one's own, and worry gnaws at what has been done and left undone.
body: Hatred (Dosa) comes from the root 'du' — to be displeased. Dosa is anger and fury: its characteristic is a fierce, coarse state of body and mind; its function is to inflame the mind, burning up and destroying its object; its manifestation is the committing of evil deeds, wrecking and harming oneself, others, or both.

Two things give rise to hatred-rooted consciousness: love of self — holding oneself dear, exalting oneself, treating oneself as the one that matters — and love of what belongs to the self, holding dear whatever is counted as one's own.

From these two, reflected through the three times, come three sets of nine resentments: the first — that person has harmed me, is harming me, will harm me; the second — that person has harmed, is harming, will harm those dear to me; the third — that person has helped, is helping, will help my enemy.
Several states keep company with hatred: sorrow (soka), lamentation (parideva), displeasure (domanassa), violence (hiṃsa), spite (palāsa), rage (kodha), terror (bherava) and fear (bhaya).

Envy (Issā), from 'i' with the root 'su', is jealousy and resentment: it cannot bear another's success, and will not tolerate another being better than oneself. Its characteristic is resenting the excellence of others; its function is dissatisfaction with what others have gained; its manifestation is turning one's face away from another's good fortune. It occurs in the two hatred-rooted cittas and goes with displeased feeling.

In practice envy springs up most readily between people of the same trade, the same circle, the same calling: the poor envy the rich, one envies another's pleasures, their gains, their faith and following, the esteem and fame they enjoy, the offerings they receive.

Avarice (Macchariya) is analysed as the root 'mā' (do not, let it not be) with 'accha' (clear, pure, showing itself): let nothing noble, fine or pure be displayed. It is stinginess, miserliness, meanness, hoarding.

Avarice hides one's own attainment and prosperity; it is unwilling to give away anything that is one's own, unwilling to share what one has; it even obstructs others from giving, grudges the sight of someone giving a fine gift, and regrets a gift once it has been made.

Five kinds of avarice are enumerated: avarice about dwelling, about family and supporters, about gain, about beauty and reputation, and about the Dhamma. Note well: refusing to give liquor or drugs that will do harm, refusing money that will be used for evil, refusing shelter to someone who intends harm — such withholding is NOT avarice.

Worry (Kukkucca), from 'ku' (bad, wrong), is the state of one who is agitated, anxious and remorseful over a wrong action: regret, uneasiness, confusion. Its characteristic is grieving over what is past; its function is to make the mind fret and smart over what has already been done.

Two things cause this inward remorse: evil that has been done, and good that has been left undone. Worry is classified in four ways: thinking what should not be done ought to be done; thinking what should be done ought not to be done; thinking what is blameless is an offence; and thinking what is an offence is blameless.

M4_S08.summary: Sloth shrinks the mind and torpor dulls the mental factors — both the opposite of energy — while doubt wavers and arises in only one citta.
body: Sloth (Thīna) is darkness and sinking: the mind sunk in gloom. Thīna comes from the root 'the' — to contract: the shrivelling of a feather before a flame, a sickly weakness, a curling up that will not act, dullness, listless laziness, loss of alertness, leaving consciousness and its factors sluggish.

The fourfold definition of sloth: its characteristic is the limpness and loss of alertness of the mind; its function is to abandon energy, so that diligence ceases; its manifestation is the mind's retreating and sinking; its proximate cause is unwise attention, mishandling the mind. The direct opposite of sloth is energy.

Torpor (Middha) is drowsiness, the nodding of sleep. Middha comes from the root 'middh' — incapacity to function: a dazed, languid, sleepy, weary state that reflects a mind no longer eager or active, and that smothers the mental factors.

Sloth and torpor always arise together, and they are found in the five prompted unwholesome cittas: the four prompted greed-rooted cittas and the one prompted hatred-rooted citta. The pair weigh down and clog the consciousness and factors they accompany — the exact opposite of the beautiful pair, lightness of mental factors and lightness of consciousness.

Doubt (Vicikicchā), analysed as 'vi' with the root 'kit' and 'cha', is uncertainty and indecision: wavering, hesitation, inability to come to a conclusion. It occurs in one citta only, the delusion-rooted citta accompanied by equanimity and associated with doubt.

Doubt is of two kinds, ordinary and special. Special doubt covers doubt about faith — is the Buddha really omniscient? does his Dhamma truly bring benefit? did he actually reach Buddhahood? — and doubt about the real nature of things, which has eight modes: doubt about the virtues of the Buddha, of the Dhamma, of the Sangha, about the three trainings (virtue, concentration, wisdom), about the past, the future, the present, and about dependent origination.

Doubt about the Buddha is listed in five points: did he truly attain omniscience? does his radiance really light up what is hidden? are the six-coloured rays said to have issued from him while he contemplated the Abhidhamma genuine and complete? how did he subdue the sectarians by his psychic power? did he in fact possess the thirty-two marks of a Great Man?
